newsitem.title: UK: Britain mounts new bid to lift beef export ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain mounts new bid to lift beef export ban.

text.p: Britain mounted a fresh attempt to end the European Union export ban on British beef on Tuesday, submitting plans to Brussels for a scheme under which cattle herds would be certified free from mad cow disease.

Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg wrote to EU farm commissioner Franz Fischler with details of the plan, urging him to move immediately so that sales of British beef, banned for 11 months, can resume as soon as possible.
Government sources said the plan addresses "a very important point" under the Florence Agreement of June last year which set out the steps Britain must take to get the ban lifted.

"I have urged the Commission to ensure that the consultation procedure laid down in the Florence Agreement is initiated immediately so that we can resume exports of meat from animals in export certified herd as soon as possible," Hogg said in a written answer to a parliamentary question.

Hogg has written to fellow EU farm ministers explaining how Britain has implemented a programme to eradicate mad cow disease (Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy) and "to seek a constructive contribution to the discussion of our proposals".

The new scheme will be considered by an EU veterinary committee, and then by farm ministers, who have previously been reluctant to sanction British exports in the light of evidence that mad cow disease is transmissible to humans.

If they approved it, Britain would have cleared the chief remaining hurdle in the way of a resumption of exports which have been halted since last March when the government admitted a fatal brain disease, CJD, could be contracted from eating beef.
Among the first farmers to benefit from a lifting of the cull would be those in Northern Ireland where much better records of cows' histories are kept.
This would please the nine Ulster Unionist members of parliament on whom Major, stripped of his parliamentary majority by by-election losses and defections, is now dependent in key votes.
Britain sees the other obstacle to the lifting of the ban as the need for a cull of an extra 100,000 cattle seen as vulnerable to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
But in Paris, a senior British meat industry official told Reuters on Monday that this cull, which is additional to the slaughter of a million cattle last year, will begin next week.
"Several hundred herds have been inspected and the selective cull will start next week," Henry Lewis, export marketing manager for Britain's Meat and Livestock Commission, said.
The opposition Labour Party has made capital out of the fact that Major promised a partial lifing of the ban by last November, but nothing happened.
However, a Labour bid to censure Hogg for his handling of the crisis proved a damp squib last week when the government won the vote on a parliamentary motion to reduce his salary by 13 votes.
